and let \(D'\) be the cofibered category over \(C^\circ\) inverse image of the cofibered category (7.2.6.1). Let \(D\) be the corresponding fibered category over \(C\), with the same fiber categories as \(D'\), so that for \(p\in\ob C\),
\[
D_p=\text{the category of right }G_p\text{-torsors}.
\]
Construct canonical functors
\begin{equation*}
D\longrightarrow C'=\Ppoint(B_G)\quav C'\longrightarrow D,\tag{7.2.6.2}
\end{equation*}
quasi-inverse to one another. In particular, conclude that the category of points of \(B_G\) lying above a given point \(p\) of \(E\) is canonically equivalent to the category of right torsors under the group \(G_p\).

\item Let \(\mathcal G=(G_i)_{i\in I}\) be a strict projective system of group objects of the \(\U\)-topos \(E\), where \(I\in\U\) is a filtered preordered set, whence a classifying topos \(B_{\mathcal G}\), imitating the definition of 2.7.1. Determine the category of points of \(B_{\mathcal G}\), imitating a). In other words, replace the categories \((\Ttors)\) and \((\text{Groups})\) by the categories of projective systems indexed by \(I\) in these categories. Conclude that if \(I\) admits a countable cofinal subset, then every fiber functor on \(B_{\mathcal G}\) is isomorphic to a functor induced by a fiber functor on \(E\), via the functor which forgets the operations of \(G\); the latter is determined up to non-unique isomorphism.

\item Take \(E\) to be the punctual topos, so that \(\mathcal G\) is an ordinary pro-group. Show that the conclusion of b) is also valid if \(I\) is arbitrary but \(\mathcal G\) is profinite, \ie\ the \(G_i\) are finite: every fiber functor is isomorphic to the functor which forgets the operations of \(G\).

\item Still in the case where \(E\) is the punctual topos, give an example of a fiber functor on \(B_{\mathcal G}\), for a suitable projective system \(\mathcal G=(G_i)_{i\in I}\), which is not isomorphic to the functor which forgets the operations of \(G\).

\item Regard \(\mathcal G=(G_i)\) as a group object of the topos \(\widehat I\), and let \(\mathcal T\) be a \emph{gerbe} on \(I\) with \emph{band} \(G\) [3]. Show how one may ``twist'' the classifying topos \(B_G\) by means of the gerbe \(T\), obtaining a topos \(B^T_{\mathcal G}\), an inductive limit of subcategories \(B^T(i)\) equivalent, non-canonically, to the classifying topoi \(B_{G_i}\). Show that the topos \(B^T_{\mathcal G}\) admits a fiber functor if and only if the gerbe \(T\) is neutral, by establishing an equivalence of categories between the category of fiber functors of \(B^T_{\mathcal G}\) and the category of sections of \(T\) over \(I\). Conclude, if the \(G_i\) are commutative, so that gerbes on \(I\) banded by \(\mathcal G\) are classified by
\[
{\varprojlim_I}^{(2)}G_i=H^2(I,\mathcal G)
\]
(\loccit), that there is an example of a topos, non-empty in the sense of 2.2, of the form \(B^T_{\mathcal G}\) which has no points. Take an example where \({\varprojlim_I}^{(2)}G_i\ne0\).
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}

\subsection*{7.3. Points of the topoi \(\widehat C\); examples of \(\U\)-topoi \(\widehat C\) whose category of points is not equivalent to a small category}

Let \(E\) be a \(\U\)-topos and let \((\varphi_i)_{i\in I}\) be a filtered family of fiber functors on \(E\). It follows from the exactness properties of the functors \(\varinjlim\) (I, 2.8) that \(\varphi=\varinjlim\varphi_i\) is again a fiber functor: \emph{every filtered inductive limit of fiber functors is a fiber functor}. Consequently the category \(\Ffib(E)\) admits \(\U\)-small filtered inductive limits, and the inclusion functor \(\Ffib(E)\to\Hhom(E,(\U\text{-}\Set))\) commutes with them. Equivalently, the category \(\Ppoint(E)\) admits \(\U\)-small filtered projective limits. This fact was already used in Exercises 7.1.10 and 7.1.11 to give examples of large categories of fiber functors.

One can construct much simpler examples, with topoi of the form \(E=\widehat C\), \(C\in\U\), using (6.8.6.1). This immediately gives examples where \(\Ffib(\widehat C)\) is not equivalent to a category belonging to \(\U\), \ie\ where the cardinality of the set of isomorphism classes of objects of this \(\U\)-category is not in \(\U\). This means that the category \(\Pro(C)\) is not equivalent to a category in \(\U\). It suffices, for example, to take \(D=C^\circ\) to be the category of finite sets of the form \([0,n]\), where \(n\ge0\) is an integer. Then \(\Ind(D)\simeq\Pro(C)^\circ\) is equivalent to the category of non-empty sets. In this case the topos \(E\) is the familiar category of \emph{cosimplicial sets}. One could also take for \(C\) the category of non-empty finite sets; then the category of points of the topos \(\widehat C\) of simplicial sets is equivalent to the category of profinite sets, or equivalently to the category of totally disconnected compact spaces.

\subsection*{7.4. Non-empty topoi without points}

The following example is due to P.~Deligne. For another example, cf. 7.2.6 e). Take a compact space \(K\) endowed with a measure \(\mu\), and the ordered set \(U\) of measurable subsets of \(K\), modulo sets of measure zero. Make \(U\) into a category \(\underline U\) with \(\ob\underline U=U\), whose morphisms are the inclusion morphisms among elements of \(U\). Make \(\underline U\) into a site by taking the pretopology in which \(\Cov(E)\), for \(E\in U\), consists of countable families of elements \(E_i\) of \(U\), bounded above by \(E\), such that \(E\) is the union of the \(E_i\), modulo a set of measure zero. One obtains a topos \(\Top(\mu)=\underline U^{\sim}\), which admits the set of subobjects of the final object as a generating family. This topos seems to have escaped the attention of probabilists. It is the empty topos (2.2) if and only if \(\mu=0\). On the other hand, the category of points of this topos is equivalent to the discrete category defined by the set of points \(x\in K\) such that \(\mu(\{x\})\ne0\). The proof is left to the reader. Thus it is empty when \(K\) has no such points, for example when \(K\) is the unit interval on the real line, with the measure induced by Lebesgue measure.

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 7.5 (Karoubian categories and geometric morphisms)}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item Let \(C\) be a category, \(X\) an object of \(C\), and \(p\) an endomorphism of \(X\). One says that \(p\) is a \emph{projector} if \(p^2=p\). Prove that, if \(p\) is a projector, then \(\Ker(\id_X,p)\) is representable if and only if \(\Coker(\id_X,p)\) is representable, and the two objects of \(C\) so obtained are canonically isomorphic. One then says that the projector \(p\) \emph{admits an image}, and \(\Ker(\id_X,p)\simeq\Coker(\id_X,p)\) is called the \emph{image of the projector \(p\)}. Depending on the context, it is identified with a subobject or with a quotient object of \(C\). An object isomorphic to \(\im p\), for a suitable projector \(p\) of \(X\), is called a \emph{direct summand of the object \(X\) of \(C\)}. One says that \(C\) is a \emph{category with direct summands}, or a \emph{Karoubian category}, if every projector in an object of \(C\) admits an image. If \(F:C\to C'\) is a functor which commutes with kernels or cokernels, then \(F\) carries a projector admitting an image to a projector admitting an image.\footnote{In fact no condition on \(F\) is needed here: all functors preserve projectors which admit images.}

\item Show that for every category \(C\) one can find a functor \(\varphi:C\to\kar(C)\) from \(C\) into a Karoubian category, determined up to equivalence, such that for every Karoubian category \(C'\), the functor
\[
f\longmapsto f\circ\varphi:\Hhom(\kar(C),C')\longrightarrow\Hhom(C,C')
\]
is an equivalence of categories. We call \(\kar(C)\) the \emph{Karoubi envelope} of \(C\). Hint: take \(\ob\kar(C)\) to be the set of pairs \((X,p)\), where \(X\in\ob C\) and \(p\) is a projector of \(X\), and take \(\Hom((X,p),(Y,q))\) to be the subset of \(\Hom(X,Y)\) formed by those \(f:X\to Y\) such that \(f=qfp\). Show that \(\varphi\) is fully faithful.

\item Let \(F:E\to E'\) be a functor from one category to another. Show that if \(F\) commutes with a certain type of inductive or projective limits, then the same holds for every direct summand of \(F\). In particular, if \(E\) and \(E'\) are \(\U\)-topoi and if \(F\) is an inverse image functor for a geometric morphism \(E'\to E\), then the same holds for every direct summand of \(F\). Hence the category \(\Hhomtop(E',E)\) is Karoubian, and in particular the category \(\Ppoint(E)\) is Karoubian.

\item Show that for every \(\U\)-category \(C\), the category \(\Ind(C)\) is Karoubian, where \(\Ind(C)\) is formed using inductive systems in \(C\) indexed by a filtered preordered set \(I\in\U\). If \(C\in\U\), use for instance the fact (7.3) that \(\Ind(C)\) is equivalent to the category \(\Ffib((C^\circ)^{\widehat{\phantom{,}}})=\Ppoint((C^\circ)^{\widehat{\phantom{,}}})^\circ\). Deduce another construction of \(\kar(C)\), as the full subcategory of \(\Ind(C)\) formed by the images in \(\Ind(C)\) of projectors of objects \(X\) of \(C\).
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 7.6 (Essential geometric morphisms; essential points)}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item Let \(f:E\to F\) be a geometric morphism. Show that the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item \(f_!\) exists, \ie\ \(f^*\) admits a left adjoint.
\item \(f^*\) commutes with \(\U\)-small projective limits.
\item \(f^*\) commutes with \(\U\)-small products.
\end{enumerate}
One then says that \(f\) is an \emph{essential morphism} of topoi from \(E\) to \(F\). Show that if \(f\) satisfies these conditions, then the same holds for every direct summand of \(f\). Use 1.8 and 7.5 c).

\item Let \(E\) be a topos. An \emph{essential point} of \(E\) is a point \(p:P\to E\) such that \(p_!\) exists. Show that if \(E=\Top(X)\), with \(X\) a topological space, and if \(p\) is the point of \(E\) defined by \(x\in X\), then \(p\) is essential if and only if \(x\) admits a smallest open neighborhood \(U\). If the points of \(X\) are closed, this means that \(x\) is an isolated point of \(X\). For a geometric morphism \(f:E\to F\) to be essential, it is necessary that \(f\) carry essential points to essential points; this condition is also sufficient when \(E\) has enough essential points, meaning when these points form a conservative family. Cf. d).

\item A point \(p\) of the topos \(E\) is essential if and only if the associated fiber functor is represented by an object \(X\) of \(E\). For the covariant functor \(\varphi:E\to(\Set)\) represented by a given object \(X\) of \(E\) to be a fiber functor, \ie\ to define a necessarily essential point of \(E\), it is necessary and sufficient that \(X\) be non-empty connected (4.3.5) and projective, \ie\ that \(\varphi\) carry epimorphisms to epimorphisms. Hint: first show that \(\varphi\) commutes with sums if and only if \(X\) is non-empty connected, then use the criterion 4.9.4. Conclude an equivalence between the category \(\Ppointess(E)\) and the full subcategory \(P\) of \(E\) formed by the non-empty connected projective objects.

\item Show that the topology on \(P\) induced by that of \(E\) is the chaotic topology. Deduce the equivalence of the following conditions on \(E\), due to J.~E.~Roos [12 c), Proposition~1]: (i) the family of essential points of \(E\) is conservative; (ii) the full subcategory \(P\) of \(E\) formed by non-empty connected projective objects is generating; (iii) \(E\) is equivalent to a topos of the form \(\widehat C\), where \(C\) is a category equivalent to a category in \(\U\), or, equivalently, one may take \(C\in\U\). Use c) and the fact that, if \(P\) is generating, the natural functor \(E\to P^{\sim}\) is an equivalence of categories.

\item The category of essential points of a topos \(E\) is Karoubian (cf. 7.5 c)). Let \(C\) be a category equivalent to a category in \(\U\). Prove that the canonical fully faithful functor (4.6.2)
\[
C\longrightarrow\Ppoint(\widehat C)
\]
factors through a functor
\[
C\longrightarrow\Ppointess(\widehat C),
\]
which makes \(\Ppointess(\widehat C)\) a \emph{Karoubi envelope} of \(C\) (7.5 b)). In particular, this functor is an equivalence of categories if and only if \(C\) is Karoubian. Hint: using c), prove that every isolated point of \(\widehat C\) is isomorphic to a direct summand of an \(X\in\ob C\).

\item Let \(C\) and \(C'\) be two categories equivalent to categories in \(\U\). Prove that the canonical fully faithful functor (4.6.2)
\[
\Hhom(C,C')\longrightarrow\Hhomtop(\widehat C,\widehat{C'})
\]
takes its values in the full subcategory \(\Hhomtopess(\widehat C,\widehat{C'})\) of essential geometric morphisms, and that the induced functor
\[
\Hhom(C,C')\longrightarrow\Hhomtopess(\widehat C,\widehat{C'})
\]
is an equivalence of categories if and only if \(C\) is empty or \(C'\) is Karoubian. Use g) below.

\item Let \(C\) be a category equivalent to a category in \(\U\), and let \(E\) be a topos. Define an equivalence between the category \(\Hhomtopess(\widehat C,E)\) of essential geometric morphisms \(\widehat C\to E\), and the category \(\Hhom(C,\Ppointess(E))\). Use b) and the fact that \(\widehat C\) has enough essential points.

\item Let \(C\) be a finite category. Prove that every point of \(\widehat C\) is essential, and that \(\Ppoint(\widehat C)\) is equivalent to a finite category. Noting that the Karoubi envelope of \(C\) is finite and using (6.8.6.1), reduce to proving that if \(C\) is a finite Karoubian category, then the canonical functor \(C\to\Pro(C)\) is an equivalence of categories. Using b), conclude that \emph{every} geometric morphism \(\widehat{C'}\to\widehat C\) is essential, and that \(\Hhom(C,C')\to\Hom(\widehat C,\widehat{C'})\) is an equivalence if and only if \(C\) is empty or \(C'\) is Karoubian.

\item Let \(X\) be a topological space, and let \(f:\Top(X)\to P\) be the geometric morphism induced by the continuous map from \(X\) to the one-point space. Show that \(f\) is essential if and only if \(X\) is \emph{locally connected}, \ie\ satisfies the following condition: for every \(x\in X\) and every open neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\), the connected component of \(x\) in \(U\) is a neighborhood of \(x\); equivalently, for every open subset \(U\) of \(X\), the connected components of \(U\) are open. Cf. 8.7 l) for a generalization.
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 7.7 (Unusual points of a classifying topos)}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item Let \(G\) be a monoid. The monoid \(G\) contains an element \(g\) such that \(g\ne e\) and \(g^2=g\) if and only if the classifying topos \(B_G\) admits an essential point not isomorphic to the trivial point, the one corresponding to the fiber functor which forgets the operations of \(G\). Use 7.6 e).
\item Let \(G\) be the additive monoid of integers \(\ge0\). Show that every essential point of the classifying topos \(B_G\) is isomorphic to the trivial point. Construct a point of \(B_G\) which is not isomorphic to the trivial point. Show that the category \(\Ppoint(B_G)\) is not equivalent to a category in \(\U\).
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 7.8 (Topology on \(\Point(E)\), and topoi associated with ordered sets)}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item Let \(E\) be a topos. Denote by \(\Point(E)\) the set of isomorphism classes of points of \(E\). For every open \(U\) of \(E\), let \(U'\) be the set of classes of points \(p\) of \(E\) such that \(U_p\ne\varnothing\). Show that \(U\mapsto U'\) is an increasing map from the ordered set \(\Ouv(E)\) of open subobjects of \(E\) to the set of subsets of \(X=\Point(E)\), and that this map commutes with finite infima and arbitrary suprema. Deduce that the subsets of \(X\) of the form \(U'\) define a topology on \(X\), called the \emph{canonical topology on the set of classes of points of the topos \(E\)}. Show that if \(E\) has enough points, the map \(U\mapsto U'\) is an isomorphism from the ordered set \(\Ouv(E)\) to the ordered set \(\Ouv(X)\).

\item Let \(\Oo\in\U\) be an ordered set admitting finite infima and arbitrary suprema; it therefore defines a category \(\cat(\Oo)\) having finite products and arbitrary sums. We say that a family of morphisms \(U_i\to U\) with common target \(U\) is covering if \(U\) is the supremum of the \(U_i\). Assuming that sums in \(\cat(\Oo)\) are universal, \ie\ that arbitrary suprema in \(\Oo\) commute with finite infima, this defines a topology on \(\cat(\Oo)\), making it a site. The resulting topos \(\cat(\Oo)^{\sim}\) is also denoted simply \(\Oo^{\sim}\). Show that \(\Oo\) is canonically isomorphic to \(\Ouv(\Oo^{\sim})\).

Show that the category \(\Hhomtop(E,\Oo^{\sim})\) is equivalent to the category associated with the ordered set of morphisms of ordered sets \(\Oo\to\Ouv(E)\) which commute with finite infima and arbitrary suprema. Use the criterion 4.9.4. If \(\Oo'\) is an ordered set satisfying the same conditions as \(\Oo\), conclude that \(\Hhomtop(\Oo^{\sim},{\Oo'}^{\sim})\) is equivalent to the category associated with the ordered set of all morphisms of ordered sets \(\Oo\to\Oo'\) which commute with finite infima and arbitrary suprema.

\item Show that for the topos \(E\) to be equivalent to a topos of the form \(\Oo^{\sim}\), with \(\Oo\) as in b), it is necessary and sufficient that the family of opens of \(E\) be generating in \(E\). For it to be equivalent to \(\Top(X)\) for \(X\in\U\), it is necessary and sufficient that it satisfy the preceding condition and have enough points. Assuming the first condition holds, express the second in terms of the structure of the ordered set \(\Oo=\Ouv(E)\), using the last assertion of b).

\item Define a canonical geometric morphism
\[
E\longrightarrow\Ouv(E)^{\sim}
\]
which is universal, up to equivalence, for morphisms from \(E\) to topoi generated by their opens (cf. c)).

\item Let \(X'\) be a small subset of \(X=\Point(E)\), endowed with the topology induced from that of \(X\). Define a canonical geometric morphism
\[
\Ouv(E)^{\sim}\longrightarrow\Top(X')
\]
which is an equivalence when the family \(X'\) of points of \(E\) is conservative. In that case, deduce a canonical geometric morphism
\[
E\longrightarrow\Top(X').
\]
Give a universal characterization, up to equivalence, of this geometric morphism for morphisms from the topos \(E\) to topoi of the form \(\Top(Y)\). Notice in this connection that, up to equivalence, \(\Top(X')\) does not depend on the small conservative family of fiber functors chosen; equivalently, by 4.2, \(X'_{\sob}\) does not depend, up to homeomorphism, on the choice of such a family.

\item Suppose that the category \(\Ppoint(E)\) is not equivalent to a small category (cf. 7.3), and that \(E\) admits a small conservative family of fiber functors. Show that if such a family is chosen sufficiently large, the subset \(X'\) of \(\Ppoint(E)\) which it defines is not a sober topological space for the induced topology.

\item For the relations with Exercise 7.6, see Section~8.
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}

\section{Localization. Opens of a topos}

\subsection*{8.1}
Let \(C\) be a category, and let \(T(X)\) be a relation involving an object \(X\) of \(C\). One says that the relation \(T(X)\) is \emph{stable under base change}, in \(X\), if for every morphism \(X'\to X\) of \(C\), the relation \(T(X)\) implies \(T(X')\). This is equivalent to saying that the full subcategory \(R\) of \(C\), formed by the objects \(X\) of \(C\) for which \(T(X)\) holds, is a \emph{sieve}.

\begin{remarktext}{Remark 8.1.1}
Suppose that \(C\) is a \(\U\)-category, so that \(C\) may be identified with a full subcategory of \(\widehat C\) (I, 1.4). It is sometimes convenient to extend the definition of the relation \(T\) on \(\ob C\) to a relation \(\widehat T\) concerning an object \(F\) of \(\widehat C\), by defining \(\widehat T(F)\) to mean: for every arrow \(X\to F\) in \(\widehat C\), with \(X\in\ob C\), one has \(T(X)\). The relation \(\widehat T(F)\) is clearly still stable under base change in \(F\). Still denoting by \(R\) the subobject of the final object \(e\) of \(\widehat C\) defined by the sieve \(R\) of \(C\) (I, 4.2.1), the relation \(\widehat T(F)\) may also be expressed by \(\Hom_{\widehat C}(F,R)\ne\varnothing\), meaning that the unique morphism \(F\to e\) factors through the subobject \(R\) of \(e\).
\end{remarktext}

\subsection*{8.2}
Now suppose that \(C\) is a \emph{site}. A relation \(T(X)\), in one argument \(X\in\ob C\), is said to be \emph{stable under descent} if, for every covering family \((X_i\to X)_{i\in I}\) of an object \(X\) of \(C\), the relation ``\(T(X_i)\) for all \(i\in I\)'' implies \(T(X)\). One says that \(T\) is a \emph{relation of local nature} if it is stable under base change (8.1) and stable under descent. When \(C\) is a \(\U\)-category, and \(T\) is already assumed stable under base change, \ie\ definable by a sieve \(R\) of \(C\), which is identified with a subpresheaf of the final presheaf on \(C\), one sees immediately that \(T\) is of local nature if and only if \(R\) is a \emph{sheaf}. Thus \emph{relations of local nature in one argument \(X\in\ob C\) correspond exactly to subsheaves of the final sheaf of \(C\), \ie\ to subobjects of the final object of the topos \(C^{\sim}\).} They therefore essentially depend only on the topos \(C^{\sim}\) defined by the site \(C\), as do all important notions associated with a site. In terms of the subsheaf \(R\) of the final sheaf, the relation \(T(X)\) is expressed as \(\Hom(\varepsilon(X),R)\ne\varnothing\). It extends canonically to the relation \(T^{\sim}(F):\Hom(F,R)\ne\varnothing\) on the topos \(C^{\sim}\).

\begin{remarktext}{Remark 8.2.1}
With the notation introduced in 8.1.1, for a presheaf \(F\) on \(C\), since \(\Hom(F,R)\simeq\Hom(a(F),R)\), the relation \(\widehat T(F)\) is equivalent to the relation \(\widehat T(a(F))\).
\end{remarktext}

\begin{statement}{Definition 8.3}
An \emph{open} of a \(\U\)-topos \(E\) is a subobject of the final object \(e_E\) of \(E\). If \(X\) is an object of \(E\), an \emph{open of \(X\)} sometimes means an open of the induced topos \(E_{/X}\), \ie\ a subobject of \(X\).

An \emph{open} of a \(\U\)-site \(C\) is an open of the associated \(\U\)-topos \(C^{\sim}\).
\end{statement}

Notice that, since final objects of \(E\) are canonically isomorphic, the ambiguity introduced in 8.3 by the choice of \(e_E\) is harmless. One may also, more intrinsically but less conveniently in practice, define the opens of \(E\) to be the full subcategories \(R\) of \(E\) such that the relation \(F\in\ob R\), for an object \(F\) of \(E\), is a relation of local nature. Likewise, the opens of a \(\U\)-site \(C\) correspond bijectively to full subcategories of \(C\) such that the relation \(F\in\ob R\), for an object of \(C\), is of local nature. Thus this notion is essentially independent of the chosen universe \(\U\). Finally, by 8.2, a relation of local nature on a topos, or on a site, is essentially the same thing as an open of that topos, or of that site.

\subsection*{8.4. Examples of opens}

\subsubsection*{8.4.1}
Let \(X\) be a topological space, and interpret \(\Top(X)\) (2.1) as the category of \'{e}tale spaces over \(X\). Since monomorphisms in \(\Top(X)\) are plainly the injective maps, it follows that the opens of the topos \(\Top(X)\) identify with the open subsets of the space \(X\). More generally, the opens of a topos \(\Top(X,G)\) (2.4) identify with the open subsets of \(X\) which are invariant under the action of \(G\).

\subsubsection*{8.4.2}
The opens of a \(\U\)-topos \(E\) form a \(\U\)-small ordered set under inclusion, admitting arbitrary suprema and finite infima. It has the initial object, or empty object, \(\varnothing_E\), as least element, and the final object \(e_E\) of \(E\) as greatest element. These two elements are identical only if \(E\) is an empty topos (2.2).

\subsubsection*{8.4.3}
Let \(G\) be a monoid object of \(E\), whence a topos \(B_G\) (2.4, 2.6), the category of objects of \(E\) on which \(G\) acts on the left. The final object \(e_G\) of \(B_G\) is the final object \(e_E\) of \(E\), with trivial action of \(G\). It follows that the ordered set of opens of \(B_G\) is canonically isomorphic to the category of opens of \(E\). In particular, if \(E\) is the punctual topos, so that \(G\) is an ordinary monoid, the set of opens of \(B_G\) consists exactly of two elements, namely \(\varnothing_{B_G}\) and \(e_G\).

\subsubsection*{8.4.4}
If \(E\) is a topos of the form \(\widehat C\), where \(C\) is a \(\U\)-category, then by 8.1 the ordered set of opens of \(E\) is isomorphic to the ordered set of sieves of \(C\).

\subsubsection*{8.4.5}
Let \(X\) be a sober non-discrete topological space. Show that \(\TOP(X)\) (2.5) has opens which do not come from opens of \(X\), \ie\ from opens of \(\Top(X)\), by inverse image under the canonical morphism (4.10.1) \(\TOP(X)\to\Top(X)\).

\subsection*{8.5. Examples of relations of local nature}

For every object \(X\) of the topos \(E\), denote by \(F\mapsto F_X\) the \emph{localization functor} \(j_X^*:E\to E_{/X}\), \(Y\mapsto Y\times X\) (5.2).

\subsubsection*{8.5.1}
Let \(u:F\to G\) be a morphism of \(E\). The relation in the argument \(X\in\ob E\):
\begin{center}
\(u_X:F_X\to G_X\) is a monomorphism, respectively an epimorphism, respectively an isomorphism,
\end{center}
is a relation of local nature. In particular, if \(G\) is a group object of \(E\), the relation ``\(G_X\) is the trivial group over \(X\)'' is of local nature; the open of \(E\) which corresponds to it is called the \emph{cosupport of the group object \(G\)}.

\subsubsection*{8.5.2}
Let \(u,v:F\rightrightarrows G\) be two morphisms of \(E\). The relation in the argument \(X\in\ob E\)
\[
u_X=v_X:F_X\longrightarrow G_X
\]
is a relation of local nature. In particular, if \(G\) is a group object of \(E\), and \(u\) is a \emph{section} of \(G\) (4.3.6), the relation in \(X\)
\begin{center}
the section \(u_X\) of the group object \(G_X\) of \(E_{/X}\) is zero
\end{center}
is of local nature; the open of \(E\) which corresponds to it is called the \emph{cosupport of the section \(u\) of the group object \(G\)}.

\begin{remarktext}{Remark 8.5.3}
When \(E=\Top(X)\), the cosupport of a sheaf of groups \(G\), respectively of a section of such a sheaf \(G\), is just the open subset of \(X\) complementary to the \emph{support of} \(G\), respectively the \emph{support of} \(u\), in the classical terminology [TF].
\end{remarktext}

\subsubsection*{8.5.4}
Let \(P(f)\) be a relation in the argument \(f\in\operatorname{Fl} C\), where \(C\) is a site. When fiber products are representable in \(C\), one says that the relation \(P(f)\) is \emph{stable under base change}, respectively \emph{stable under descent}, respectively \emph{of local nature}, \emph{on the target}, or \emph{on the base}, or ``downstairs'', if for every morphism \(f:X\to Y\) of \(C\), the relation in the argument \(Y'\in\ob C_{/Y}\):
\begin{center}
the morphism \(f':X'=X\times_Y Y'\to Y'\), obtained from \(f\) by base change along the structural morphism \(Y'\to Y\), satisfies \(P(f')\),
\end{center}
is stable under base change, respectively stable under descent, respectively is of local nature. When the topology of \(C\) is defined by a pretopology, one says that the relation \(P(f)\) is \emph{of local nature on the source}, or ``upstairs'', if for every morphism \(f:X\to Y\) of \(C\) and every family \((g_i:X_i\to X)_{i\in I}\) in \(\Cov(X)\), the relation \(P(f)\) is equivalent to the relation ``\(P(fg_i)\) for all \(i\in I\)''. When \(\Cov(X)\) consists of all covering families of \(C\), this condition also says that the relation in the object \(X'\) of the induced site \(C_{/X}\),
\begin{center}
\(P(fg)\), where \(g:X'\to X\) is the structural morphism,
\end{center}
is of local nature. Notice that if \(P(f)\) is of local nature upstairs, then it is a fortiori of local nature downstairs.

\subsubsection*{8.5.5}
For example, take \(C=(\Sch)\), the category of schemes belonging to \(\U\), with the faithfully flat quasi-compact topology (\SGA~3, IV, 6.3) or a less fine topology. Then each of the following properties of a morphism is of local nature on the target:
\begin{center}
\begin{minipage}{0.93\linewidth}
surjective, radicial, universally open, universally closed, proper, quasi-compact, quasi-compact and dominant, universal homeomorphism, separated, quasi-separated, locally of finite type, locally of finite presentation, of finite type, of finite presentation, an isomorphism, a monomorphism, an open immersion, a closed immersion, a quasi-compact immersion, affine, quasi-affine, finite, quasi-finite, integral, flat, faithfully flat, unramified, smooth, \'{e}tale.
\end{minipage}
\end{center}
See \EGA~IV, 2.6.4, 2.7.1, and \EGA~IV, 17.7.1. On the other hand, endow \((\Sch)\) with the pretopology for which, for every scheme \(X\in\U\), \(\Cov(X)\) consists of families of morphisms \((f_i:X_i\to X)_{i\in I}\) which are surjective and such that the \(f_i\) are flat and locally of finite presentation. Then each of the following properties is \emph{of local nature on the source}:
\begin{center}
locally of finite type, locally of finite presentation, of finite type, flat, unramified, smooth, \'{e}tale.
\end{center}
See \EGA~IV, 17.7.5, 17.7.7.

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 8.6}
Let \(f:E\to F\) be a morphism of \(\U\)-topoi. Consider the relation in the argument \(X\in\ob F\): the induced morphism \(E_{/f^*(X)}\to F_{/X}\) is an equivalence of topoi. Prove that this relation is of local nature.
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 8.7 (Partitions of a topos; sums of topoi)}
Let \(E\) be a \(\U\)-topos. A family \((e_i)_{i\in I}\) of opens of \(E\), \ie\ of subobjects of the final object \(e\) of \(E\), is called a \emph{partition of} \(e\), or of the topos \(E\), if the canonical morphism \(\coprod_{i\in I}e_i\to e\) is an isomorphism; equivalently, by II, 4.6.2, \(e\) is the supremum of the \(e_i\) and \(i\ne j\) implies \(e_i\cap e_j=\varnothing_E\).
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item Show that a family \((e_i)_{i\in I}\) of objects of \(E\) is a partition of \(E\) if and only if the functor
\begin{equation*}
E\longrightarrow\prod_i E_{/e_i}\tag{8.7.1}
\end{equation*}
defined by the localization functors \(E\to E_{/e_i}\) is an equivalence of categories.

\item Conversely, let \((E_i)_{i\in I}\) be a family of \(\U\)-topoi, with \(I\in\U\). Prove that \(E=\prod_{i\in I}E_i\) is a \(\U\)-topos, called the \emph{sum topos} of the family \((E_i)_{i\in I}\). Define a partition \((e_i)_{i\in I}\) of \(E\), and equivalences of categories \(E_{/e_i}\simeq E_i\), in such a way that the projection functors \(E\to E_i\) identify with the localization functors \(E\to E_{/e_i}\).

\item Let \(E\) be the sum topos of the family \((E_i)_{i\in I}\). Show that for every \(i\in I\) the projection functor \(E\to E_i\) has the form \(u_i^*\), where
\begin{equation*}
u_i:E_i\longrightarrow E\tag{8.7.2}
\end{equation*}
is a geometric morphism. Prove that for every \(\U\)-topos \(F\), the functor \(v\mapsto(v\circ u_i)_{i\in I}\)
\begin{equation*}
\Hhomtop(E,F)\longrightarrow\prod_i\Hhomtop(E_i,F)\tag{8.7.3}
\end{equation*}
is an equivalence of categories.

\item Let \((e_i)_{i\in I}\) be a partition of the topos \(E\). For every geometric morphism \(g:F\to E\), the family \((f_i)_{i\in I}\), with \(f_i=g^*(e_i)\), is a partition of \(F\), and the induced morphisms \(g_i:E_{/e_i}\to F_{/f_i}\) allow one to reconstruct \(g\), up to unique isomorphism; the functor \(g^*\) identifies with the Cartesian product of the functors \(g_i^*\), using the equivalences of type 8.7.1. Deduce a complete description of the category \(\Hhomtop(F,E)\) in terms of categories of the form \(\Hhomtop(F',E_i)\), where \(F'\) is a topos of the form \(F_{/f}\), with \(f\) a direct summand of the final object of \(F\), and \(E_i=E_{/e_i}\).

\item In particular, if \(F\) is non-empty connected (cf. 4.3.5), \ie\ if for every partition \((f_i)_{i\in I}\) of \(F\) there is exactly one \(i\in I\) with \(f_i\ne\varnothing_F\), prove that the canonical functor
\begin{equation*}
\coprod_{i\in I}\Hhomtop(F,E_i)\longrightarrow\Hhomtop(F,E)\tag{8.7.4}
\end{equation*}
induced by the geometric morphisms (8.7.2) is an equivalence of categories. More particularly, the family of geometric morphisms (8.7.2) induces an equivalence of categories
\[
\coprod_{i\in I}\Ppoint(E_i)\xrightarrow{\sim}\Ppoint(E).
\]

\item A subset \(I\) of the set of opens of \(E\) is called a \emph{reduced partition} of \(E\) if the identical family \((e_i)_{i\in I}\), indexed by \(I\), is a partition and if each \(e_i\ne\varnothing_E\). Show that the refinement relation (I, 4.3.2) among reduced partitions makes the set \(P\) of reduced partitions into a \(\U\)-small ordered set such that the least upper bound of two elements of \(P\) exists. Thus one obtains a strict projective system \((I_p)_{p\in P}\), regarded as a pro-set and denoted \(\pi_0(E)\). It is called the \emph{pro-\(\pi_0\) of the topos} \(E\).

\item Prove that \(\pi_0(E)\) pro-represents the functor
\[
T\longmapsto f_*f^*(T)=\Gamma(E,T_E):(\U\text{-}\Set)\longrightarrow(\U\text{-}\Set)
\]
associated with the canonical morphism \(f:E\to P\) from \(E\) to the punctual topos \(P\) (4.3). In particular, this functor is representable if and only if \(\pi_0(E)\) is essentially constant, \ie\ isomorphic, as a pro-set, to an ordinary set, again denoted \(\pi_0(E)\). The pro-set \(\pi_0(E)\) is reduced to one point if and only if \(E\) is non-empty connected. It is empty if and only if \(E\) is the empty topos (2.2).

\item Suppose that \(E\) is quasi-compact, \ie\ every covering of its final object \(e\) admits a finite subcovering. Show that \(\pi_0(E)\) is then a profinite set, and may therefore be identified, via the well-known equivalence between pro-objects of the category of finite sets and totally disconnected compact spaces, with a totally disconnected compact space, also denoted \(\pi_0(E)\).

\item Let \(X\) be a topological space, and let \(\pi_0(X)\) be the set of connected components of \(X\), regarded as a constant pro-set. Define a canonical morphism of pro-sets
\begin{equation*}
\pi_0(X)\longrightarrow\pi_0(\Top(X)),\tag{8.7.5}
\end{equation*}
or equivalently a canonical map
\begin{equation*}
\pi_0(X)\longrightarrow\varprojlim\pi_0(\Top(X)).\tag{8.7.6}
\end{equation*}
Show that the first morphism is an isomorphism if and only if \(X\) is homeomorphic to a sum space of connected spaces. This is the case in particular if \(X\) is locally connected.

\item Suppose that \(X\) is a quasi-compact scheme. Prove that (8.7.6) is bijective.

\item Establish the functorial character in \(X\) of the morphisms (8.7.5) and (8.7.6), beginning by specifying the meaning of this expression.

\item Compare 7.6 i). Show that the following two conditions on the \(\U\)-topos \(E\) are equivalent: (i) the canonical morphism from \(E\) to the punctual topos is essential (Exercise 7.6 a)), \ie\ the functor \(I\mapsto I_E\) from \((\U\text{-}\Set)\) to \(E\) commutes with products indexed by sets belonging to \(\U\); (ii) for every object \(X\) of \(E\), the induced topos \(E_{/X}\) has a \(\pi_0(E_{/X})\) which is an ordinary set, \ie\ \(X\) is isomorphic to the sum of a family of connected objects of \(E\). One then says that \(E\) is a \emph{locally connected topos} (compare IV, 2.7.5).
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 8.8 (Dominant geometric morphisms)}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item Let \(f:E'\to E\) be a geometric morphism. Show that the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item \(f_*(\varnothing_{E'})=\varnothing_E\), where \(\varnothing_E\) and \(\varnothing_{E'}\) denote the initial objects of \(E\) and \(E'\).
\item For every object \(X\) of \(E\) which is non-empty, \ie\ not isomorphic to \(\varnothing_E\), the object \(f^*(X)\) is non-empty in \(E'\).
\item As in (ii), with \(X\) a subobject of the final object \(e_E\) of \(E\), \ie\ an open of the topos \(E\).
\end{enumerate}
One then says that the geometric morphism \(f\) is \emph{dominant}.

\item Let \(f:X'\to X\) be a continuous map of topological spaces, whence a geometric morphism \(\Top(f):\Top(X')\to\Top(X)\) (4.1). Show that \(\Top(f)\) is dominant if and only if \(f\) is dominant, \ie\ \(f(X')\) is dense in \(X\).

\item Show that if \(f:E'\to E\) is a conservative geometric morphism (6.4.0), \ie\ if \(f^*\) is faithful, then \(f\) is dominant. Show that the converse is not necessarily true, even for a localization morphism \(E_{/U}\to E\), where \(U\) is an open of the topos \(E\). In this case, show that \(f\) is conservative only if \(U\) is the final object of \(E\), hence only if \(f\) is an equivalence of topoi, and use the example b).

\item Let \(f:X'\to X\) be an arrow in a topos \(E\). One says that \(f\) is a \emph{dominant morphism} in the topos \(E\) if the corresponding morphism of induced topoi \(E_{/X'}\to E_{/X}\) (5.5.2) is dominant. Show that this property depends only on the image \(f(X')\) of \(X'\) in \(X\), as an element of the ordered set \(\ouv(X)\) of subobjects of \(X\). Show that the morphism \(E_{/X'}\to E_{/X}\) is conservative if and only if \(f\) is covering.
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}


\clearpage
\section*{SGA 4, Exposé IV, Section 9}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{SGA 4, Exposé IV, Section 9}

\bigskip

\section*{9. Subtopoi and gluing of topoi}

\subsection*{9.1. Subtopoi and embeddings of topoi}

\begin{statement}{Definition 9.1.1}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item A morphism of topoi \(f:F\to E\) is called an \emph{embedding} if the functor
\(f_*:F\to E\) is fully faithful, or equivalently if the adjunction morphism
\(f^*f_*\to \id_F\) is an isomorphism.

\item A \emph{subtopos} of a topos \(E\) is a strictly full subcategory \(E'\) of \(E\) which is a topos and for which the inclusion functor
\(\alpha:E'\to E\) is of the form \(i_*\), where \(i:E'\to E\) is a morphism of topoi; equivalently, \(\alpha\) has a left adjoint \(i^*\) which is left exact. The morphism \(i\), determined up to unique isomorphism, is then called the \emph{inclusion morphism} of the subtopos \(E'\) into \(E\).
\end{enumerate}
\end{statement}

\begin{remarktext}{Remark 9.1.2}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item The inclusion morphism of a subtopos is an embedding. A strictly full subcategory \(E'\subset E\) is a subtopos if and only if it is the essential image of the direct-image functor \(f_*\) attached to a morphism of topoi \(f:F\to E\) which is an embedding.

\item A morphism \(f:F\to E\) of topoi is an embedding if and only if it is isomorphic to a composite
\[
F\xrightarrow{g} E'\xrightarrow{i} E,
\]
where \(g\) is an equivalence of topoi and \(i\) is the inclusion of a subtopos \(E'\) of \(E\). The subtopos \(E'\), namely the essential image of \(f_*\), is uniquely determined, and the factorization is unique up to unique isomorphism. In practice one identifies \(F\), by means of \(g\), with the corresponding subtopos of \(E\).

\item An equivalence of topoi \(u:E\xrightarrow{\sim}E_1\) gives, in the evident way, a bijection between the subtopoi of \(E\) and the subtopoi of \(E_1\). Thus for the study of subtopoi one may reduce to the case \(E=\widetilde C\), where \(C\) is a small site. In that case a strictly full subcategory \(E'\subset E\) is a subtopos if and only if its inclusion has a left exact left adjoint. Moreover the subtopoi so obtained correspond bijectively to the topologies \(T'\) on \(C\) finer than the given topology \(T\): to \(T'\) one associates the strictly full subcategory \((C,T')^\sim\) of \(C^\sim\) consisting of the sheaves for \(T'\). Consequently, for any \(\U\)-topos \(E\), a strictly full subcategory \(E'\subset E\) is a subtopos if and only if its inclusion has a left exact left adjoint; the ordered set \(\mathfrak E(E)\) of subtopoi of \(E\) is \(\U\)-small, and every subset of it admits a supremum and an infimum.

\item If \(E'\) and \(E''\) are two subtopoi of \(E\), their intersection is again a subtopos. In the case \(E=C^\sim\), let \(T'\) and \(T''\) be the corresponding topologies on \(C\), both finer than \(T\). Then \(E'\cap E''\) is the category of sheaves for the topology \(T'''\) which is the supremum of \(T'\) and \(T''\). More generally, if \(T'\) is the supremum of a family \((T_i)\) of topologies, then the sheaves for \(T'\) form the intersection of the corresponding categories of sheaves.
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}

\begin{statement}{Proposition 9.1.3}
For every family \((E_i)_{i\in I}\) of subtopoi of a topos \(E\), the intersection
\[
\bigcap_{i\in I}E_i
\]
is a subtopos of \(E\).
\end{statement}

\begin{statement}{Proposition 9.1.4}
Let \(i:E'\to E\) be an embedding of topoi, and let \(F\) be a topos. The functor
\[
f\longmapsto i\circ f:\Hhomtop(F,E')\longrightarrow \Hhomtop(F,E)
\tag{9.1.4.1}
\]
is fully faithful. Its essential image consists of those morphisms \(g:F\to E\) for which the essential image of \(g_*\) is contained in that of \(i_*\).
\end{statement}

\begin{prooftext}
Consider the evident commutative square
\[
\xymatrix@C=1.75cm@R=1cm{
\Hhomtop(F,E')\ar@{^{(}->}[d]\ar[r]&\Hhomtop(F,E)\ar@{^{(}->}[d]\\
\Hhom(F,E')\ar[r]&\Hhom(F,E).
}
\]
The vertical functors send a morphism of topoi to its direct image and are fully faithful by definition of \(\Hhomtop\). Since \(i_*\) is fully faithful, the lower horizontal functor is fully faithful, and so is the upper one. The characterization of the image follows from \((if)_*=i_*f_*\). Conversely, if \(g_*=i_*f_*\) for a functor \(f_*:F\to E'\), then \(f_*\) has the left adjoint \(g^*i_*\), which is left exact; hence \(f_*\) is the direct image of a morphism of topoi \(f:F\to E'\).
\end{prooftext}

\begin{statement}{Corollary 9.1.5}
If \(f:E'\to E\) is an embedding of topoi, then the induced functor on categories of points
\[
\Point(f):\Ppoint(E')\longrightarrow \Ppoint(E)
\tag{9.1.5.1}
\]
is fully faithful.
\end{statement}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 9.1.6. Embeddings of topoi and \(2\)-monomorphisms}
Let \(i:E'\to E\) be a morphism of topoi.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item If \(F\) and \(G\) are topoi over \(E'\), define the canonical functor
\[
f\longmapsto f*i:\mathcal{H}om_{\mathrm{top},E'}(F,G)\longrightarrow \mathcal{H}om_{\mathrm{top},E}(F,G).
\tag{9.1.6.1}
\]
\item Suppose that \(i\), as a \(1\)-arrow of the \(2\)-category of topoi, is a \(2\)-monomorphism, that is, for every topos \(F\) belonging to a sufficiently large universe the functor (9.1.4.1) is fully faithful. Show that for every pair of topoi \(F,G\) the functor (9.1.6.1) is fully faithful.
\item Show that \(i\) is an embedding if and only if \(i\) is a \(2\)-monomorphism.
\item Let \(g:F\to E\) be a morphism of topoi and assume the \(2\)-fiber product
\[
F'=F\times_E^2 E'
\]
exists. Let \(j:F'\to F\) be the projection. If \(i\) is an embedding, show that \(j\) is an embedding. When \(E'\) is a subtopos of \(E\), the essential image of \(j_*\) is called the \emph{inverse-image subtopos of \(F\)} of \(E'\) by \(g\).
\item With the preceding notation, let \(X\) be an object of \(F\). Show that if \(X\) belongs to the inverse-image subtopos \(F'\), then for every object \(U\) of \(F\), writing \(g_U:F_{/U}\to E\) for the induced morphism and \(X|U=(X\times U\to U)\), one has
\[
g_{U*}(X|U)\in \Ob E'.
\]
Ask conversely whether this condition is sufficient, or equivalently whether the strictly full subcategory so obtained is a subtopos of \(F\).
\item If \(X\in E\), put \(X'=i^*X\) and let \(i_{/X}:E'_{/X'}\to E_{/X}\) be the induced morphism of topoi. Show that if \(i\) is an embedding, then \(i_{/X}\) is an embedding. Conversely, if \((X_\alpha)_\alpha\) is a covering family of the final object and every \(i_{/X_\alpha}\) is an embedding, then \(i\) is an embedding.
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 9.1.7. Subtopoi and multiplicative sets of arrows}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item Let \(i:E'\to E\) be a morphism of topoi and let \(S\) be the set of arrows \(u\) of \(E\) such that \(i^*(u)\) is an isomorphism. Let
\[
\rho:E[S^{-1}]\longrightarrow E'
\tag{9.1.7.1}
\]
be the canonical functor induced by \(i^*\). Show that \(i\) is an embedding if and only if \(\rho\) is an equivalence. In this case \(S\) admits both a left and a right calculus of fractions. The essential image of \(i_*\) consists of the objects \(X\in E\) such that, for every \(u:Y\to Y'\) in \(S\), the map
\[
\Hom(Y',X)\longrightarrow\Hom(Y,X)
\]
is bijective.

\item Assume now that \(i\) is an embedding. For any topos \(F\), show that the functor
\[
f^*\longmapsto f^*i^*:\Hhom(E',F)\longrightarrow\Hhom(E,F)
\]
induces an equivalence between inverse-image functors arising from morphisms \(F\to E'\) and inverse-image functors \(g^*:E\to F\) arising from morphisms \(F\to E\) which carry every arrow of \(S\) to an isomorphism.

\item Let \(S\subset \Fl(E)\). Show that \(S\) comes from a subtopos by the preceding construction if and only if it satisfies:
\begin{itemize}
\item[ST1)] \(S\) contains the isomorphisms and is stable under composition and base change.
\item[ST2)] If a composite \(vu\) lies in \(S\), then \(u\in S\) if and only if \(v\in S\).
\item[ST3)] If \(u:X\to Y\) becomes an element of \(S\) after base change by a covering family \(Y_i\to Y\), then \(u\in S\).
\end{itemize}
This gives a bijection between subtopoi of \(E\) and subsets \(S\subset\Fl(E)\) satisfying ST1--ST3. Given \(S\), associate to it the topology \(T'\) finer than the canonical topology for which \((X_i\to X)\) is covering precisely when the image of \(\coprod X_i\to X\) is included by a monomorphism belonging to \(S\).

\item \(S\) is determined by its monomorphisms. The assignment \(S\mapsto S_0\), where \(S_0\) is the subset of monomorphisms in \(S\), gives a bijection between subsets of \(\Fl(E)\) satisfying ST1--ST3 and subsets of monomorphisms satisfying the same conditions.

\item If \((E_i')_{i\in I}\) is a family of subtopoi and \(S_i\) are the corresponding subsets of \(\Fl(E)\), then \(\bigcap_i S_i\) satisfies ST1--ST3 and corresponds to the subtopos generated by the \(E_i'\), that is, to their supremum.

\item Given \(A\subset\Fl(E)\), there is a smallest subset \(S\supset A\) satisfying ST1--ST3. It is the union of subsets \(A_n\), \(n\ge 0\), obtained inductively by adjoining isomorphisms, composites, base changes, factors of composites whose other factor and composite are already present, small sums, and arrows which become present after an epimorphic base change.
\item With the notation of e), if \(A=\bigcup_iS_i\) and \(S\) is obtained from \(A\) as in f), then the corresponding subtopos is the intersection, or infimum, of the \(E_i'\).
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 9.1.7.2. Canonical factorization of a morphism of topoi}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item Let \(f:F\to E\) be a morphism of topoi. Show that, up to isomorphism, \(f\) factors as
\[
F\xrightarrow{f'}E'\xrightarrow{i}E,
\tag{9.1.7.3}
\]
where \(f'\) is conservative and \(i\) is an embedding; this factorization is unique up to equivalence. Introduce \(S_f\subset\Fl(E)\), the arrows \(u\) such that \(f^*u\) is an isomorphism, and take for \(E'\) the subtopos associated with \(S_f\).

\item The subtopos defined by \(i\) is called the \emph{image subtopos} of \(f\). It is the smallest subtopos through which \(f\) factors, or equivalently the smallest subtopos containing the essential image of \(f_*\). The morphism \(f\) is an embedding if and only if it induces an equivalence of \(F\) with its image; it is conservative if and only if its image is all of \(E\).

\item Suppose \(f=\Top(f_0)\) comes from a continuous map \(f_0:Y\to X\) of sober spaces. Let \(Y\to X'=f_0(Y)\to X\) be the usual factorization. The canonical factorization of \(f\) is the corresponding factorization
\[
\xymatrix@C=2cm{\Top(Y)\ar[r]&\Top(X')\ar@{^{(}->}[r]&\Top(X).}
\]
If \(Z\) is the smallest sober subspace of \(X\) containing \(f_0(Y)\), then \(f\) is conservative if and only if \(Z=X\), that is, if \(f_0(Y)\) is very dense in \(X\). Thus conservative morphisms of topoi generalize surjective continuous maps.

\item Give a \(2\)-cartesian square of topoi
\[
\xymatrix{F'\ar[r]\ar[d]&F\ar[d]^f\\E'\ar[r]&E}
\]
with \(f\) conservative but \(f'\) not conservative, for instance \(E'\) a punctual topos and \(F'\) the empty topos.

\item For a family \((E_i)_{i\in I}\) of subtopoi of \(E\), prove that \(E=\bigvee_iE_i\) if and only if the family of embedding morphisms \(E_i\to E\) is conservative.
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 9.1.8. Subtopoi and points; the case of topological spaces}
Let \(E\) be a topos.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item Let \(Z\) be a full subcategory of \(\Ppoint(E)\), or the corresponding subset of isomorphism classes of points. Define \(E_Z\) to be the intersection of all subtopoi \(E'\) of \(E\) through which every point of \(Z\) factors. Show that \(E_Z\) is the smallest such subtopos.
\item If \((Z_i)\) is a family of such full subcategories, show that \(E_{\bigcup_iZ_i}\) is the subtopos generated by the \(E_{Z_i}\).
\item If \(E'\subset E\), describe the full subcategory of points of \(E\) coming from \(E'\), and show that \(E'\subset E_Z\) exactly when the points of \(Z\) factor through \(E'\).
\item Let \(E=\Top(X)\) for a sober space \(X\). For a sober subspace \(X'\subset X\), the associated subtopos \(E_{X'}\) is the essential image of \(\Top(X')\to\Top(X)\). Conversely, every subtopos with enough points is of this form.
\item If \((X_i')\) is a family of sober subspaces of \(X\), there is a smallest sober subspace \(X'\) containing them; it is the union when the family is finite or when \(X\) is separated. The subtopos \(E_{X'}\) is generated by the \(E_{X_i'}\).
\item Give an example of a subtopos of a topos of the form \(\Top(X)\) which is nonempty but has no points.
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 9.1.9. Topoi defined by ordered sets}
Use the dictionary between topoi generated by their open subobjects and ordered sets admitting arbitrary suprema, finite infima, and distributivity of finite infima over arbitrary suprema.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item If \(f:E'\to E\) is an embedding and \((X_i)\) is a generating family of \(E\), then \((f^*X_i)\) is a generating family of \(E'\). Thus a subtopos of a topos generated by its opens is again generated by its opens.
\item Let \(f:E'\to E\) be a morphism of such topoi, corresponding to a morphism \(g:\Oo\to\Oo'\) of ordered sets. Show that \(f\) is an embedding if and only if \(g\) is surjective and also surjective on the graphs of the order relations; equivalently, the order on \(\Oo'\) is the quotient of the order on \(\Oo\).
\item If \(E=\Oo^\sim\), subtopoi correspond to equivalence relations \(R\) on \(\Oo\) compatible with finite infima and arbitrary suprema. Under this correspondence, the subtopos generated by a family corresponds to the intersection of the corresponding equivalence relations.
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 9.1.10. Intersections of subspaces, point-free topoi, and nonexistence of complements}
Let \(X\) be a topological space and \(E=\Top(X)=\Ouv(X)^\sim\).
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item Define \(R\) on \(\Ouv(X)\) by \((U,U')\in R\) if \(U\cap U'\) is dense in both \(U\) and \(U'\). Show that \(R\) satisfies the conditions of 9.1.9 and defines a subtopos \(E'\). A point \(x\) of \(X\) comes from \(E'\) if and only if it is \emph{thick}, that is, belongs to the closure of the interior of \(\overline{\{x\}}\). The subtopos \(E'\) is empty only when \(X\) is empty.
\item If \(X\) is sober, \(\Ppoint(E')\) is equivalent to the ordered set of thick points. If the points of \(X\) are closed, the thick points are precisely the isolated points; hence a nonempty separated space without isolated points gives a nonempty subtopos without points.
\item If \(X'\subset X\) and \(E_{X'}\) is as in 9.1.8, then for dense \(X'\), \(E_{X'}\) contains the preceding \(E'\). If \(X\) is sober and \(X'\), \(X''\) are sober subspaces, then \(X'\cap X''\) is sober and
\[
E_{X'\cap X''}\subset E_{X'}\cap E_{X''},
\]
and the inclusion may be strict. It is an equality exactly when the right-hand side has enough points; this holds if one of \(X'\), \(X''\) is locally closed.
\item Let \(X''=X-X'\). If \(X''\) is a union of locally closed subsets, then the subtopoi disjoint from \(E_{X'}\) have a largest element, the \emph{weak complement} of \(E_{X'}\), precisely when \(E_{X'}\cap E_{X''}\) is empty. If this fails, the infimum in the ordered set of subtopoi is not distributive over arbitrary suprema.
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 9.1.11. Subtopoi of locally noetherian topoi}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item If \(f:E'\to E\) is an embedding and \(X\) is a prenoetherian object of \(E\), then \(f^*X\) is prenoetherian. Hence if \(E\) has a generating family of prenoetherian objects, or is noetherian or locally noetherian, then \(E'\) has the same property.
\item If \(E\) is locally noetherian, every subtopos of \(E\) is of the form \(E_Z\) for a suitable full subcategory \(Z\) of \(\Ppoint(E)\). In particular, if \(E=\Top(X)\) with \(X\) sober and locally noetherian, then \(Z\mapsto E_Z\) identifies sober subspaces of \(X\) with subtopoi of \(E\), and intersections of sober subspaces correspond to intersections of subtopoi.
\item For \(X\) sober locally noetherian and \(X'\subset X\), with complement \(X''\), the following are equivalent: \(X'\) is constructible; both \(X'\) and \(X''\) are sober; \(E_{X'}\) has a complementary subtopos; and \(E_{X'}\cap E_{X''}\) is empty.
\item For \(X\) sober noetherian, the following are equivalent: every sober subspace is constructible; it is enough to test \(X-\{x\}\) for maximal \(x\); \(X\) is finite; every subtopos of \(\Top(X)\) has a complement; and infima distribute over arbitrary suprema.
\item If \(X\) is locally noetherian, then in the ordered set of subtopoi of \(\Top(X)\) finite suprema distribute over binary infima.
\item For every sober subspace \(Z\) of a sober locally noetherian \(X\), define a topology \(T_Z\) on \(\Ouv(X)\) by declaring \((U_i\to U)\) covering when \(U\cap Z=\bigcup_i(U_i\cap Z)\). Then \(Z\mapsto T_Z\) is an order-reversing bijection from sober subspaces of \(X\) to topologies on \(\Ouv(X)\) finer than the canonical topology.
\item For a sober topological space \(X\), a subset is sober if and only if its complement is a union of locally closed subsets. If \(X\) is locally noetherian this is the same as proconstructibility. The constructible topology \(X_{\cons}\) identifies the ordered set of subtopoi of \(\Top(X)\) with the closed subsets of \(X_{\cons}\); complemented subtopoi correspond to clopen subsets.
\item If \(E\) is locally noetherian and has the property stated in 9.1.14 b), then the essential images of \(\Ppoint(E')\to\Ppoint(E)\), with \(E'\) running over all subtopoi, are the closed subsets of a topology \(T_{\cons}\) on the set of isomorphism classes of points, and the ordered set of subtopoi is identified with these closed subsets.
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 9.1.12. Finite topoi}
A topos \(E\) is called \emph{finite} if it is equivalent to \(\widehat C\) for a finite category \(C\).
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item There are quasi-inverse \(2\)-equivalences between Karoubian categories equivalent to finite categories and finite topoi:
\[
C\longmapsto\widehat C,\qquad E\longmapsto\Ppoint(E).
\]
\item A finite topos is noetherian.
\item If \(E\simeq\widehat C\), with \(C\) Karoubian and finite up to equivalence, then subtopoi of \(E\) correspond to strictly full Karoubian subcategories \(C'\subset C\). The subtopos is the essential image of \(\widehat{C'}\to\widehat C\).
\item The finite set \(X=\Point(E)\) of isomorphism classes of points carries a canonical sober topology, for which subtopoi of \(E\) correspond to closed subsets of \(X\). Thus the ordered set of subtopoi is finite.
\item For a category \(C\) equivalent to a finite category and a full subcategory \(C'\), define a topology \(T_{C'}\) by declaring \((X_i\to X)\) covering when, for every \(Y\in C'\), the maps \(\Hom(Y,X_i)\to\Hom(Y,X)\) are jointly surjective. This gives an order-reversing bijection from strictly full Karoubian subcategories of \(C\) to topologies on \(C\).
\item If \(f:C'\to C\) and \(C\) is equivalent to a finite category, then \(\widehat f:\widehat{C'}\to\widehat C\) is conservative if and only if every object of \(C\) is a direct factor of an object in the image of \(f\).
\item For the category with objects \(e,a\) and arrows \(f:a\to e\), \(g:e\to a\), \(p=gf\), \(p^2=p\), show that \(\widehat C\) has exactly one proper nonempty subtopos, namely \(\widehat{\{e\}}\). Thus any two nonempty subtopoi meet nontrivially.
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 9.1.13. Complementary subtopoi}
Two subtopoi \(E'\), \(E''\) of \(E\) are called \emph{complementary} if
\[
E'\cap E''=\emptytopos,\qquad E'\vee E''=E.
\]
Assume binary infima distribute over finite suprema in the ordered set of subtopoi.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item If \(E'\) and \(E''\) are complementary, then \(E''\) is the largest subtopos disjoint from \(E'\).
\item The following are equivalent: every weak complement is a complement; every proper subtopos has a nonempty disjoint subtopos; every maximal subtopos disjoint from a given one is a complement. These conditions may fail even for finite topoi, but hold for \(\Top(X)\) with \(X\) locally noetherian.
\item Complemented subtopoi are stable under finite infima, finite suprema, and complements; complementation interchanges infima and suprema.
\item State the dual assertions.
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{9.1.14. Open questions}
Let \(E\) be a topos.
\begin{itemize}
\item[a)] In the ordered set of subtopoi of \(E\), is the infimum of two elements distributive over finite suprema?
\item[b)] If \(E'\vee E''=E\), is every point of \(E\) isomorphic to the image of a point of \(E'\) or of \(E''\)?
\item[c)] If \(E'\) and \(E''\) are subtopoi of a topos \(F\) whose supremum is \(F\), equivalently if
\[
E'\amalg E''\longrightarrow F
\tag{9.1.14.1}
\]
is conservative, is this morphism universally conservative, that is, still conservative after every \(2\)-base change?
\item[d)] In the ordered set \(\Sigma\) of subtopoi of \(E\), is the infimum of two elements distributive over arbitrary suprema?
\item[e)] If \(F\) is noetherian and \((E_i)_{i\in I}\) is a family of subtopoi with intersection \(\emptytopos\), does a finite subfamily already have empty intersection?
\end{itemize}
Positive answers to a) and d) were later supplied in the literature cited in the French edition.
\end{remarktext}

\subsection*{9.2. The case of open subtopoi}

Let \(U\) be an open of \(E\), i.e. a subobject of the final object \(e\). The localization morphism
\[
j:E_{/U}\longrightarrow E
\tag{9.2.2}
\]
is an embedding. An embedding is called an \emph{open embedding} if it is isomorphic to one so obtained; the corresponding subtopos is an \emph{open subtopos}. The open \(U\) attached to an open embedding \(j:E'\to E\) is uniquely determined as the subobject \(j_!(e')\subset e\), where \(e'\) is the final object of \(E'\). Thus opens of \(E\) are in bijection with open subtopoi of \(E\).

\begin{remarktext}{Remark 9.2.3}
The open subtopos defined by \(U\) is the essential image of \(j_*:E_{/U}\to E\). It must not be confused with the essential image of \(j_!\), namely the objects whose structural morphism to \(e\) factors through \(U\). These two subcategories determine one another and are canonically equivalent, but the former is the subtopos in the sense fixed here.
\end{remarktext}

\begin{statement}{Proposition 9.2.4}
Let \(j:\Uu\to E\) be an open embedding. Then \(j_!\), left adjoint to \(j^*\), exists; hence there is a chain of adjoint functors
\[
j_!,\quad j^*,\quad j_*.
\]
Moreover:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item \(j_!\) and \(j_*\) are fully faithful.
\item \(j_!\) commutes with fiber products, with products indexed by nonempty small sets, and with projective limits over small cofiltered categories.
\item For every \(X\in E\), the adjunction morphism \(j_!j^*X\to X\) is a monomorphism.
\end{enumerate}
\end{statement}

\begin{prooftext}
For the localization defined by an open \(U\), the functor \(j_!\) is the forgetful functor. The assertions follow from the fact that \(U\to e\) is a monomorphism and monomorphisms are stable under base change.
\end{prooftext}

\begin{remarktext}{Remark 9.2.4.1}
There are embeddings \(j:E'\to E\) for which \(j_!\) exists, but \(j_!\) does not commute with binary products or cofiltered projective limits.
\end{remarktext}

Let \(g:E'\to E\) be any morphism of topoi and put \(U'=g^*U\). The square
\[
\xymatrix@C=2cm@R=1.5cm{
E'_{/U'}\ar[d]_{g_U}\ar[r]^{j'}&E'\ar[d]^g\\
E_{/U}\ar[r]^j&E
}
\]
is \(2\)-cartesian. Thus inverse images of open subtopoi are open subtopoi, and open embeddings are stable under \(2\)-base change. Moreover, \(g\) factors through \(E_{/U}\) if and only if \(U'=e_{E'}\).

For two opens \(U,V\) of \(E\), the \(2\)-fiber product of \(E_{/U}\) and \(E_{/V}\) over \(E\) is \(E_{/U\cap V}\). Hence finite intersections of open subtopoi are open. The assignment \(U\mapsto E_{/U}\) also commutes with arbitrary suprema.

\subsection*{9.3. Construction of the closed subtopos complementary to an open subtopos}

Let \(T\) be a topological space, \(U\subset T\) an open, and \(Y=T-U\) the closed complement. Then \(\Top(Y)\) may be regarded as the subtopos of \(\Top(T)\) consisting of objects whose restriction to \(U\) is the final object. This description makes sense for any topos \(E\) and open \(U\subset e\), and it defines the closed subtopos complementary to \(U\).

Let
\[
j:\Uu=E_{/U}\longrightarrow E
\tag{9.3.2.1}
\]
be the localization. For \(X\in E\), define
\[
X_{\complement U}=U\coprod_{U\times X}X,
\tag{9.3.2.2}
\]
where the amalgamation is along the projections \(U\times X\to U\) and \(U\times X\to X\). Thus
\[
\xymatrix@C=1.75cm@R=1.5cm{
U\times X\ar[r]^{\pr_2}\ar[d]_{\pr_1}&X\ar[d]\\
U\ar[r]&X_{\complement U}
}
\tag{9.3.2.3}
\]
is cocartesian.

\begin{statement}{Proposition 9.3.3}
With the preceding notation:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item For \(X\in E\), the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item \(X\simeq Y_{\complement U}\) for some \(Y\in E\);
\item \(X\to X_{\complement U}\) is an isomorphism;
\item \(X\times U\to U\) is an isomorphism, equivalently \(j^*X\) is final in \(E_{/U}\).
\end{enumerate}
\item For a morphism \(m:X\to X'\), the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*')]
\item the square
\[
\xymatrix{X\ar[r]^m\ar[d]&X'\ar[d]\\
X_{\complement U}\ar[r]&X'_{\complement U}}
\]
is cartesian;
\item \(m\times\id_U:X\times U\to X'\times U\) is an isomorphism, equivalently \(j^*m\) is an isomorphism.
\end{enumerate}
\item The functor \(X\mapsto X_{\complement U}\) is left exact, sends epimorphic families to epimorphic families, and commutes with filtered inductive limits and pushouts.
\end{enumerate}
\end{statement}

\begin{prooftext}
First prove the assertion when \(E=\widehat C\) and reduce, by the usual arguments, to the punctual topos \(\Set\), where it is immediate. The general case follows by the standard sheafification procedure.
\end{prooftext}

\begin{statement}{Proposition 9.3.4}
Let \(\Ff\) be the strictly full subcategory of \(E\) consisting of objects \(X\) such that \(j^*X\) is final in \(\Uu\). Then \(\Ff\) is a subtopos of \(E\). Its inclusion \(i:\Ff\to E\) has inverse-image functor
\[
i^*X=X_{\complement U}.
\]
The adjunction morphism \(X\to i_*i^*X\) is the canonical morphism \(X\to X_{\complement U}\).
\end{statement}

\begin{prooftext}
Let \(u(X):X\to X_{\complement U}\). This morphism is functorial in \(X\), and \(u(X_{\complement U})\) is an isomorphism. These properties formally give an adjunction \(i^*\dashv i_*\), with \(i^*(X)=X_{\complement U}\). Since \(i^*\) is left exact, the general criterion for a full subcategory to be a topos applies.
\end{prooftext}

The subtopos \(\Ff\) is called the \emph{closed subtopos of \(E\) complementary to the open \(U\)}. Its inclusion \(i:\Ff\to E\) is a \emph{closed embedding}. Conversely a subtopos is called closed if it is obtained in this way. The complementary open is recovered as \(i_*(\varnothing_\Ff)\subset e_E\). For a group object \(G\) on \(E\), and for a section \(s\in\Hom(e_E,G)\), the \emph{support} of \(G\) or \(s\) is the closed subtopos complementary to its cosupport.

With \(j:\Uu\to E\) and \(i:\Ff\to E\), we have the two adjoint strings
\[
\xymatrix@C=2cm@R=1.5cm@M=.2cm{
\Uu\ar@<6pt>[r]^{j_!}\ar@<-13pt>[r]_{j_*}&
E\ar@<3pt>[r]^{i^*}\ar@<4pt>[l]_{j^*}&
\Ff\ar@<13pt>[l]_{i_*}.}
\tag{9.3.6.2}
\]
The functor
\[
\rho=i^*j_*:\Uu\longrightarrow\Ff
\tag{9.3.6.3}
\]
is called the \emph{gluing functor} relative to \(U\). More generally, a functor \(\rho:\Uu\to\Ff\) between topoi is called a gluing functor if it is left exact and accessible, equivalently if it admits a pro-adjoint.

\subsection*{9.4. First properties of the closed subtopos \(\Ff\)}

\begin{statement}{Proposition 9.4.1}
With the preceding notation:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item \(i_*:\Ff\to E\) sends epimorphic families to epimorphic families and commutes with pushouts and filtered inductive limits.
\item If \(X\in E\) and \(U\times X\to U\) is an epimorphism, then \(X\to i_*i^*X\) is an epimorphism.
\item The pair of functors \((i^*,j^*)\) from \(E\) to \(\Ff\) and \(\Uu\) is conservative.
\item The gluing functor \(\rho=i^*j_*:\Uu\to\Ff\) is left exact and accessible; equivalently it admits a pro-adjoint
\[
\sigma:\Pro(\Ff)\longrightarrow\Pro(\Uu).
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{statement}

\begin{prooftext}
The assertions follow directly from 9.3.3 and the construction of \(X_{\complement U}\). For d), \(j_*\) is a direct image functor and is accessible, while \(i^*\) commutes with inductive limits; the composite is therefore accessible.
\end{prooftext}

\begin{statement}{Proposition 9.4.2}
For any topos \(E'\), the functor
\[
h\longmapsto i\circ h:\Homtop(E',\Ff)\longrightarrow\Homtop(E',E)
\]
is fully faithful. Its essential image consists of those morphisms \(g:E'\to E\) such that \(g^*(U)\) is an initial object of \(E'\).
\end{statement}

\begin{prooftext}
Full faithfulness is 9.1.4. The criterion follows by writing \(U'=g^*U\) and considering the square
\[
\xymatrix@C=1.5cm{
E'_{/U'}\ar[r]^{j'}\ar[d]_{g_U}&E'\ar[d]^g\\
E_{/U}\ar[r]^j&E.
}
\]
The condition that \(g_*(X')\) lie in \(\Ff\) for all \(X'\) is equivalent to \(g_{U*}(Y')\) being final for every \(Y'\in E'_{/U'}\), and by adjunction this is equivalent to \(U'\) being initial in \(E'\).
\end{prooftext}

\begin{statement}{Corollary 9.4.3}
Let \(g:E'\to E\) be a morphism of topoi, let \(U'=g^*U\), and let \(\Ff'\) be the closed subtopos of \(E'\) complementary to \(U'\). Then \(g\circ i':\Ff'\to E\) factors, up to isomorphism, through a morphism \(g_\Ff:\Ff'\to\Ff\), and the square
\[
\xymatrix@C=2cm@R=1.4cm{
\Ff'\ar[r]^{i'}\ar[d]_{g_\Ff}&E'\ar[d]^g\\
\Ff\ar[r]^i&E
}
\tag{9.4.3.1}
\]
is \(2\)-cartesian.
\end{statement}

Thus inverse images of closed subtopoi are closed subtopoi.

\begin{statement}{Corollary 9.4.4}
Let \(\Uu\) be an open subtopos of \(E\) and \(\Ff\) its closed complement.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item
\[
\Uu\cap\Ff\simeq\emptytopos,\qquad \Uu\vee\Ff=E.
\]
Thus \(\Uu\) and \(\Ff\) are complementary subtopoi.
\item \(\Uu\) is the largest subtopos \(E'\) with \(E'\cap\Ff\simeq\emptytopos\), and \(\Ff\) is the largest subtopos \(E'\) with \(\Uu\cap E'\simeq\emptytopos\).
\end{enumerate}
\end{statement}

\begin{prooftext}
The first assertion reduces to the criteria 9.2.5 and 9.4.2 for a morphism to factor through the open or through the closed complement. The equality \(\Uu\vee\Ff=E\) is equivalent to conservativity of \((i^*,j^*)\). The maximality statements follow by applying 9.4.3 to a subtopos \(E'\subset E\).
\end{prooftext}

\begin{statement}{Corollary 9.4.5}
If \((\Ff_i)_{i\in I}\) is a family of closed subtopoi of \(E\), and \(U_i\) is the complementary open of \(\Ff_i\), then \(\bigcap_i\Ff_i\) is closed and its complementary open is \(U=\Sup_i U_i\).
\end{statement}

\begin{statement}{Corollary 9.4.6}
If the family in 9.4.5 is finite, then the supremum \(\bigvee_i\Ff_i\) is closed and its complementary open is \(\bigcup_iU_i\).
\end{statement}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 9.4.7. Gluing subtopoi}
Let \(E'\) be a subtopos of \(E\), and let \((S_i)_{i\in I}\) be a covering family of the final object of \(E\). Write \(E_i=E_{/S_i}\) and \(E_i'\) for the inverse-image subtopos of \(E'\) in \(E_i\). Show that an object \(X\in E\) belongs to \(E'\) if and only if every restriction \(X|S_i\) belongs to \(E_i'\). Conversely, if subtopoi \(E_i'\subset E_i\) are compatible on overlaps \(E_{/S_i\times S_j}\), construct a unique subtopos \(E'\subset E\) inducing them.
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 9.4.8. Exterior, closure, interior, and boundary}
For a subtopos \(E'\subset E\), define its exterior as the largest open subtopos disjoint from \(E'\), its closure as the closed complement of this exterior, its interior as the largest open subtopos contained in \(E'\), and its boundary as the closed complement of the union of the exterior and the interior. Show the expected formal properties, including compatibility with induced topoi. The exterior of \(E'\) is empty exactly when the embedding \(E'\to E\) is dominant.
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 9.4.9. Locally closed subtopoi}
A subtopos \(F\) of \(E\) is \emph{locally closed} if it is the intersection of an open subtopos and a closed subtopos.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item Finite intersections of locally closed subtopoi are locally closed, and inverse images of locally closed subtopoi are locally closed.
\item For \(E=\Top(X)\), locally closed subsets \(X'\subset X\) give locally closed subtopoi \(T(X')\); conversely, under sobriety assumptions, every locally closed subtopos comes in this way.
\item A subtopos \(F\subset E\) is locally closed if and only if it is open in its closure. This is a local property on \(E\).
\item Among all expressions \(F=\Uu\cap\Ff\) with \(\Uu\) open and \(\Ff\) closed, there is a canonical one with \(\Uu\) largest and \(\Ff\) smallest, namely \(\Ff=\overline F\) and \(\Uu\) the largest open inducing \(F\) on \(\Ff\).
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 9.4.10}
Develop the notions of constructible, locally constructible, quasi-constructible, and locally quasi-constructible subtopoi on the model of the analogous notions for topological spaces. For \(E=\Top(X)\), these notions recover the corresponding classes of subsets of \(X\).
\end{remarktext}

\subsection*{9.5. The gluing theorem}

Let \(f:A\to B\) be a functor. Denote by \((B,A,f)\) the category whose objects are triples \((X,Y,u)\), with \(X\in B\), \(Y\in A\), and \(u:X\to f(Y)\); a morphism \((X,Y,u)\to(X',Y',u')\) is a pair \((m,m')\), with \(m:X\to X'\), \(m':Y\to Y'\), such that
\[
\xymatrix@C=1.5cm@R=1cm{
X\ar[r]^u\ar[d]_m&f(Y)\ar[d]^{f(m')}\\
X'\ar[r]^{u'}&f(Y')
}
\]
commutes. This construction is functorial in \(A,B,f\); in particular a natural transformation \(f\to f'\) gives a functor \((B,A,f)\to(B,A,f')\), an isomorphism if the transformation is one.

Return to \(E\), an open subtopos \(\Uu\), its closed complement \(\Ff\), and \(\rho=i^*j_*:\Uu\to\Ff\). To \(X\in E\) attach
\[
(i^*X,\ j^*X,\ h(X):i^*X\to \rho j^*X),
\]
where \(h(X)\) is obtained by applying \(i^*\) to \(X\to j_*j^*X\). This defines a functor
\[
\Phi:E\longrightarrow(\Ff,\Uu,\rho).
\tag{9.5.3.1}
\]

\begin{statement}{Theorem 9.5.4}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item Let \(E\) be a topos, \(\Uu\) an open subtopos, and \(\Ff\) its closed complement. Then \(\rho=i^*j_*:\Uu\to\Ff\) is left exact and accessible, and
\[
\Phi:E\longrightarrow(\Ff,\Uu,\rho)
\]
is an equivalence of categories.
\item Conversely, if \(\Uu\), \(\Ff\) are topoi and \(\rho:\Uu\to\Ff\) is a gluing functor, then \(E=(\Ff,\Uu,\rho)\) is a topos. The object
\[
U=(\varnothing_\Ff,e_\Uu,\varnothing_\Ff\to\rho(e_\Uu))
\]
defines an open subtopos equivalent to \(\Uu\), and the functor
\[
Y\longmapsto (Y,e_\Uu,Y\to\rho(e_\Uu))
\]
identifies \(\Ff\) with the closed complement. The resulting gluing functor is compatible with the given \(\rho\).
\end{enumerate}
\end{statement}

\begin{statement}{Definition 9.5.5}
For topoi \(\Uu,\Ff\) and a gluing functor \(\rho:\Uu\to\Ff\), the topos \((\Ff,\Uu,\rho)\) is called the topos obtained by \emph{gluing} \(\Uu\) and \(\Ff\) by means of \(\rho\).
\end{statement}

\begin{prooftext}\emph{Proof of 9.5.4 a).} 
The pair \((i^*,j^*)\) is conservative, so \(\Phi\) is faithful. For every \(X\in E\), the square
\[
\xymatrix@C=2.5cm{
X\ar[r]\ar[d]&j_*j^*X\ar[d]\\
i_*i^*X\ar[r]&i_*i^*j_*j^*X
}
\tag{*}
\]
is cartesian, by 9.3.3. Given a morphism between \(\Phi(X)\) and \(\Phi(Y)\), the universal property of this cartesian square produces a unique \(X\to Y\), showing full faithfulness. Conversely, an object \((Y,X,u:Y\to i^*j_*X)\) of \((\Ff,\Uu,i^*j_*)\) is obtained from the fiber product
\[
\xymatrix@C=2.75cm@R=1.25cm{
W\ar[r]\ar[d]&j_*X\ar[d]\\
i_*Y\ar[r]^{i_*u}&i_*i^*j_*X.
}
\]
Then \(\Phi(W)\simeq(Y,X,u)\), so \(\Phi\) is essentially surjective.
\end{prooftext}

\begin{prooftext}\emph{Proof of 9.5.4 b).} 
It remains chiefly to see that \((\Ff,\Uu,\rho)\) is a topos. Finite projective limits are computed componentwise, since \(\rho\) is left exact. Sums are constructed by
\[
\coprod_i(Y_i,X_i,u_i)=
\left(\coprod_iY_i,\ \coprod_iX_i,\ \coprod_iY_i\to\rho(\coprod_iX_i)\right),
\]
using the canonical map \(\coprod_i\rho(X_i)\to\rho(\coprod_iX_i)\). Equivalence relations are effective and universal by applying the corresponding assertions in \(\Ff\) and \(\Uu\). Finally, accessibility of \(\rho\), or equivalently the existence of a pro-adjoint \(\sigma:\Pro(\Ff)\to\Pro(\Uu)\), supplies a small generating family: take generators \(C'\) of \(\Uu\), \(C''\) of \(\Ff\), represent each \(\sigma(X'')\) by a small filtered projective system, and use the objects
\[
(\varnothing_\Ff,X',\varnothing_\Ff\to\rho X')\quad\text{and}\quad
(X'',\sigma(X'')_i,X''\to\rho(\sigma(X'')_i)).
\]
\end{prooftext}

For \(E=(\Ff,\Uu,\rho)\), the structural functors are explicitly:
\[
i^*(X,Y,u)=X,\qquad
i_*(X)=(X,e_\Uu,X\to\rho(e_\Uu)),
\]
\[
j^*(X,Y,u)=Y,\qquad
j_!(Y)=(\varnothing_\Ff,Y,\varnothing_\Ff\to\rho(Y)),
\]
\[
j_*(Y)=(\rho(Y),Y,\id_{\rho(Y)}).
\]
The adjunction morphisms are the evident morphisms represented by the arrows \(u:X\to\rho(Y)\) and by the maps to \(\rho(e_\Uu)\).

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 9.5.9. Exactness properties of a glued topos}
Let \(E=(\Ff,\Uu,\rho)\).
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item Show that \(j_!\) preserves all inductive limits and \(j^*\) preserves both all inductive limits and finite projective limits. Show that \(i^*\) preserves inductive limits, and \(i_*\) preserves filtered inductive limits and pushouts. If \(\rho\) preserves a given class of projective limits, then \(j_*\) preserves it.
\item Give an example where \(j_!\) is not exact on the right for arbitrary embeddings, and one where \(j_!\) fails to preserve products.
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 9.5.10}
Let \(E=(\Ff,\Uu,\rho)\), and let \(A\) be an object of \(E\) corresponding to \((B,C,u)\). Describe the induced topos \(E_{/A}\) as a glued topos built from \(\Ff_{/B}\) and \(\Uu_{/C}\), and identify its gluing functor.
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 9.5.11. Morphisms from a glued topos}
Let \(F\) be a category or a topos.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item Describe \(\Hhom(F,E)\) as a category glued from \(\Hhom(F,\Uu)\) and \(\Hhom(F,\Ff)\), with gluing functor induced by \(\rho\).
\item A functor \(f:F\to E\) commutes with a given class of inductive limits if and only if \(j^*f\) and \(i^*f\) do; for projective limits also require \(\rho\) to commute with them.
\item If \(F\) is a topos, then \(f\) is an inverse-image functor of a morphism \(E\to F\) if and only if \(j^*f\) and \(i^*f\) are. Hence \(\Hhomtop(E,F)\) is equivalent to the category of triples \((f',f'',u)\), where \(f'\in\Hhomtop(\Uu,F)\), \(f''\in\Hhomtop(\Ff,F)\), and \(u:{f''}^*\to\rho\,{f'}^*\) is a morphism of functors \(F\to\Ff\).
\item Spell out in what sense this gives a characterization of \(E\), up to equivalence in the \(2\)-category of topoi, by the triple \((\Uu,\Ff,\rho)\).
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 9.5.12. Gluing of topological spaces}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*)]
\item Let \(X\) be a topological space and \(\rho:\Top(X)\to\Set\) a gluing functor, represented by a pro-object \(A\in\Pro(\Top(X))\). Show that the glued topos is of the form \(\Top(Y)\) if and only if \(A\) is isomorphic to an object of \(\Pro(\Ouv(X))\). If \(X\ne\varnothing\), there are choices of \(\rho\) for which the glued topos is not of the form \(\Top(Y)\).
\item More generally, for \(\rho:\Top(X)\to\Top(Y)\), use the pro-adjoint \(\sigma\) to obtain a map
\[
\phi:X\longrightarrow \Ob\Pro(\Top(Y)).
\]
If the glued topos is \(\Top(Z)\), then \(\phi\) takes values in the essential image of \(\Pro(\Ouv(Y))\).
\end{enumerate}
\end{remarktext}

\begin{remarktext}{Problem}
Does the converse in 9.5.12 b) hold?
\end{remarktext}

\subsection*{9.6. The gluing sheaf}

The data of a topos \(E\) with an open \(U\) is, by 9.5.4, essentially the same as the data of two topoi \(\Uu\), \(\Ff\) and a gluing functor
\[
\rho:\Uu\longrightarrow\Ff,
\tag{9.6.1}
\]
or equivalently a pro-adjoint
\[
\sigma:\Pro(\Ff)\longrightarrow\Pro(\Uu).
\tag{9.6.2}
\]
The functor \(\sigma\) is determined by its restriction
\[
\sigma_\circ:\Ff\longrightarrow\Pro(\Uu),
\tag{9.6.3}
\]
extended to filtered projective limits. Conversely, \(\sigma_\circ\) arises from a pro-adjoint exactly when, for every \(X\in\Uu\), the functor
\[
Y\longmapsto \Hom_{\Pro(\Uu)}(\sigma_\circ(Y),X)
\]
on \(\Ff^{\circ}\) is representable, equivalently a sheaf for the canonical topology. Thus the opposite functor
\[
\sigma_\circ^{\circ}:\Ff^\circ\longrightarrow\Pro(\Uu)^\circ\subset\check{\Uu}=\Hhom(\Uu,\Set)
\tag{9.6.4}
\]
is a sheaf on \(\Ff\) with values in \(\Pro(\Uu)^\circ\). The data of a gluing functor is therefore equivalent to such a sheaf. This sheaf is called the \emph{gluing sheaf} attached to \(\rho\), or to the open \(U\) of \(E\).

\begin{remarktext}{Exercise 9.6.5}
Refine 9.5.4 to a statement of \(2\)-equivalence between the \(2\)-category of pairs \((E,U)\), where \(E\) is a topos and \(U\) an open, and the \(2\)-category of triples \((\Uu,\Ff,\rho)\) with \(\rho\) a gluing functor. Give the corresponding variant where \(\rho\) is replaced by the gluing sheaf \(\phi\) on \(\Ff\) with values in \(\Pro(\Uu)^\circ\).
\end{remarktext}

\subsection*{9.7. Points of a glued topos}

Let \(C\) be a category, and let \(D'\to C\), \(D''\to C\) be fully faithful functors with essential images \(C'\), \(C''\), such that the objects of \(C\) are partitioned by \(C'\) and \(C''\), and such that
\[
\Hom(X'',X')=\varnothing\qquad(X'\in C',\ X''\in C'').
\]
